papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Safety Assessment of Large Language Models Across Languages
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety evaluation of large language models (LLMs) in multilingual contexts and specific languages, highlighting the necessity for comprehensive safety benchmarks. It introduces multilingual safety assessments, particularly for non-English languages, and emphasizes the importance of safety in the deployment of LLMs. The studies reveal that LLMs tend to produce more unsafe responses in non-English queries and propose methods to enhance safety through improved prompting techniques.
literature_themes.limitations: The studies primarily focus on specific languages and may not cover all potential safety issues across all languages. There is also a limitation in the generalizability of findings, as the benchmarks are based on a limited set of safety scenarios and may not encompass all real-world applications. Additionally, the reliance on existing LLMs for safety evaluation may introduce biases based on their training data.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies a significant research gap in the safety assessment of LLMs in non-English languages and the need for multilingual safety benchmarks. It supports the identification of areas where further research is required to improve safety measures and alignments for diverse linguistic contexts, ultimately contributing to the responsible deployment of AI technologies.

literature_themes.theme: Few-Shot Recommender Systems and Language Models

literature_themes.limitations: The cluster lacks comprehensive empirical evaluations and may not address the scalability of the proposed methods in real-world applications. Additionally, the absence of detailed abstracts limits the understanding of specific methodologies used.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the potential of leveraging advanced language models in recommendation systems, indicating a research gap in the exploration of their effectiveness and adaptability in diverse recommendation contexts.

summary: Recent literature emphasizes the importance of interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs) to improve safety and controllability. Researchers propose methods to visualize and understand these representations, which can help identify biases and mitigate risks associated with LLM outputs. Techniques such as attention visualization and feature attribution are highlighted as effective tools for enhancing model transparency and ensuring alignment with human values.
scholarly_positioning: While prior approaches have made strides in visualizing internal representations of large language models (LLMs) through techniques like attention visualization and feature attribution, they often fall short in providing comprehensive frameworks for safety and controllability. Existing methods primarily focus on surface-level interpretations, leaving unresolved tensions regarding the deeper understanding of model biases and their implications for ethical AI deployment. This research aims to bridge these gaps by developing more robust interpretability frameworks that not only enhance transparency but also align LLM outputs with human values in a systematic manner. By situating this work within the broader discourse on AI safety, it addresses the urgent need for methodologies that ensure LLMs are both interpretable and controllable in real-world applications.
research_scope: This study will investigate the effectiveness of a novel interpretability framework for large language models (LLMs) in the domain of automated content generation for news articles. The target population will include professional journalists and content creators who utilize LLMs in their workflow. The AI intervention will involve a newly developed visualization tool that enhances the transparency of LLM outputs by providing real-time feedback on internal representations and biases. The study period will span six months, during which participants will use the tool in their daily tasks. A control group will utilize standard LLMs without the interpretability enhancements. Primary outcomes will include the accuracy of content generation and the perceived safety of the outputs, while secondary outcomes will assess user satisfaction and the identification of biases in generated content.
gap: Prior studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of attention visualization and feature attribution in enhancing the interpretability of large language models (LLMs) in various applications; however, they treat the integration of these interpretability techniques into practical workflows for content generation as secondary, leaving unclear whether enhanced transparency directly affects user perceptions of safety and bias identification in real-world scenarios; this matters practically because ensuring that journalists can trust LLM outputs is crucial for ethical content creation; therefore, this study investigates the impact of a novel interpretability framework on the safety and controllability of LLM-generated news articles within the defined scope.
question: How does the implementation of a novel interpretability framework for large language models affect the perceived safety and accuracy of LLM-generated news articles among professional journalists compared to standard LLM outputs?
theoretical_mechanism: The intervention involves a novel interpretability framework for large language models (LLMs), which serves as the independent variable. This framework enhances the transparency of LLM outputs through real-time feedback on internal representations and biases, acting as a psychological mechanism that influences journalists' trust and understanding of the model. The intermediate behavior is the increased engagement and scrutiny of the generated content by journalists, leading to improved accuracy and perceived safety of the outputs. The primary outcome is the quality and reliability of LLM-generated news articles, measured through user satisfaction and bias identification. The theoretical framework is grounded in the principles of transparency and trust in AI systems, with assumptions that enhanced interpretability will lead to greater user confidence and ethical content creation, requiring empirical validation.
hypothesis: The implementation of a novel interpretability framework for large language models will lead to higher perceived safety and accuracy of LLM-generated news articles among professional journalists compared to standard LLM outputs, mediated by increased engagement and scrutiny of the generated content.

Construct Operationalization Table:

| Construct Name            | Role        | Measurement Instrument         | Data Source               | Timing                |
|--------------------------|-------------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|-----------------------|
| Interpretability Framework| IV          | Visualization tool usage logs | Tool usage by journalists | Throughout study period|
| Perceived Safety         | DV          | Survey (Likert scale)        | Journalist feedback       | Post-intervention      |
| Perceived Accuracy       | DV          | Survey (Likert scale)        | Journalist feedback       | Post-intervention      |
| Engagement               | Mediator    | Content review logs          | Journalist interaction    | Throughout study period|

Causal Pathway:
The interpretability framework (IV) enhances transparency, leading to increased engagement and scrutiny (mediators) of LLM outputs, which in turn improves perceived safety and accuracy (DVs) of the generated news articles.

Likely Confounds:
Potential confounding variables include prior experience with LLMs, individual journalist biases, and external pressures (e.g., deadlines, editorial standards) that may affect perceptions independently of the interpretability framework.

Claim Boundaries:
The study claims that the interpretability framework improves perceived safety and accuracy among journalists. However, it does not claim that this framework will universally enhance all aspects of LLM outputs or that all journalists will respond similarly.

What Cannot Be Concluded:
The study cannot conclude that the interpretability framework will lead to objective improvements in the actual quality of news articles, nor can it generalize findings beyond the specific population of professional journalists involved in the study.
methodology: This study will employ a three-arm design with professional journalists as participants, comparing a novel interpretability framework for LLMs (intervention group), standard LLMs (active control), and a usual-care group using traditional content generation methods (passive control). Participants will engage with the interpretability tool over six months, during which usage logs will be collected to measure engagement and scrutiny. Perceived safety and accuracy will be assessed through post-intervention surveys using a Likert scale. The study will control for confounding variables such as prior experience with LLMs and individual biases by collecting demographic data and conducting baseline assessments. Statistical analyses, including ANOVA and regression models, will be employed to evaluate differences between groups, ensuring reproducibility and robustness of findings. The scope is limited to professional journalists to maintain focus on practical implications in content generation.
novelty_contribution: Theoretically, this research introduces a comprehensive interpretability framework that integrates real-time feedback on internal representations and biases, addressing the limitations of existing methods that focus on surface-level interpretations. Methodologically, the study employs a three-arm design that rigorously compares the effects of the novel framework against standard LLMs and traditional content generation methods, providing robust empirical evidence on user engagement and trust. Practically, the intervention aims to enhance the safety and controllability of LLM outputs in journalistic contexts, ensuring ethical content creation by fostering transparency and user confidence. This contribution extends beyond merely applying AI to journalism by systematically evaluating the impact of interpretability on user perceptions and content quality, thereby advancing knowledge in AI safety and ethical deployment in real-world applications.

proposal: This research proposes to investigate the effectiveness of a novel interpretability framework for large language models (LLMs) in enhancing safety and controllability during automated content generation for news articles, specifically targeting professional journalists who face ethical challenges in their workflows. Recent literature highlights the inadequacies of existing interpretability techniques, such as attention visualization and feature attribution, which often fail to address user perceptions of safety and bias in practical contexts, thus creating a gap in understanding how these methods can be integrated into journalistic practices. The central research question is: How does the implementation of a novel interpretability framework for LLMs affect the perceived safety and accuracy of LLM-generated news articles among professional journalists compared to standard LLM outputs? The theoretical mechanism posits that the interpretability framework (independent variable) enhances transparency, leading to increased engagement and scrutiny (mediators) of LLM outputs, which in turn improves perceived safety and accuracy (dependent variables). The falsifiable hypothesis states that the implementation of this framework will result in higher perceived safety and accuracy of LLM-generated news articles compared to standard outputs, measured through post-intervention surveys using a Likert scale and content review logs for engagement. The methodology employs a three-arm design comparing the novel framework, standard LLMs, and traditional content generation methods, with controls for prior experience and individual biases. Expected contributions include a comprehensive interpretability framework that integrates real-time feedback, robust empirical evidence on user engagement and trust, and practical implications for ethical content creation in journalism. Key limitations include potential confounding variables such as prior experience with LLMs and individual biases, along with the risk of misinterpretation of findings if no significant differences are observed. The study aims to clarify the role of interpretability in fostering trust and ethical journalism, thereby advancing knowledge in AI safety and deployment in real-world applications.
